name: Wirangu
confidence_why: one confirmed first-hand source; 5 other works read were silent
catalog_quote: The regular accent in Wirangu is on the first syllable of a word, as is the case in all the surrounding languages. It is a fairly heavy stress accent ... The accent is accompanied by a high pitch intonation. There is a secondary stress on the third syllable of words of more than three syllables ... In emphatic vocatives and imperatives the accent can shift to the final syllable

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification

audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-strict', initial primary stress with secondary on the third syllable (stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 10100 (1 = a stressed syllable)), rests directly on Hercus 1999:35, the sole reference grammar, which we hold and whose statement I confirmed verbatim at the stated section and page. Hercus states the pattern for the third syllable only; the alternating continuation for 5+ syllables in the rule string is an extrapolation but consistent with her description and with her note that disyllabic suffixes carry secondary stress. The documented exceptions (emphatic vocative/imperative final shift; optional stress on derived long aa in -(g)ardu forms) are pragmatic/optional and already captured in the domain quotation, so they do not threaten the fixed: initial syllable classification. sources.quote: "The regular accent in Wirangu is on the first syllable of a word, as is the case in all the surrounding languages. It is a fairly heavy stress accent... The accent is accompanied by a high pitch intonation. There is a secondary stress on the third syllable of words of more than three syllables... There are however a few situations in which this can vary. In emphatic vocatives and imperatives the accent can shift to the final syllable" (Hercus 1999:35, §2.2.2(a).
